narrative:
The model predicted a 62% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in the third year of law school had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the third decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. Your first-year performance ranked second in importance and also pulled the outcome toward failure; again, a third-decile ranking falls well below the sixth-decile average of admitted students. Your family income bracket came third. Being in the upper-middle income group slightly increased the predicted risk of failure relative to other brackets in the applicant pool.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed your solid LSAT score of 34, your 3.10 undergraduate GPA, and the fact that you plan to attend full-time. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or pursue additional relevant experience that demonstrates sustained high performance. Consider reapplying once you can show clearer evidence of ability to succeed on the bar exam.
